newsitem.title: USA: Johnson Controls reaches tentative pact with UAW.
newsitem.headline: Johnson Controls reaches tentative pact with UAW.

text.p: Johnson Controls Inc. said Thursday it reached a tentative contract agreement with the United Auto Workers union, bringing an end to a 24-day strike that disrupted production of one of Ford Motor Co.'s most profitable vehicles.
The contract covers about 500 workers at seat assembly plants in Plymouth and Oberlin, Ohio. Workers at the plants will be asked to ratify the contracts within two days, the company said.
Details were not released, but company officials said the agreements will provide wages and benefits that are comparable to those in place at other Johnson Control facilities.
The officials said the contracts, the first for the two plants since workers joined the UAW last year, are fair and reasonable in terms of the Johnson Controls' business goals.

"The wage and benefit packages that have been tentatively accepted by the UAW are very much within the range of what we expected for the labour markets in the Plymouth and Oberlin areas," said Chip McClure, general manager for Johnson Controls.
A UAW spokesman could not be reached for comment.
The union had been pressing for the company to pledge neutrality in organising attempts at other plants. But a source close to the strike said the contract does not include any neutrality language.
Workers went on strike Jan. 28 when talks broke down. The UAW has said it wants base pay levels equal to the $14 to $16 an hour that competitor Lear Corp. pays.

The Plymouth plant employs about 300 hourly workers and produces seating systems for the Ford Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle. The Oberlin plant employs about 200 hourly workers and produces seating systems for the Econoline and Club Wagon full-size vans.

Ford refused to accept seats made by non-union replacements, but it continued to build vehicles, believing the strike would be over soon. But after building close to 15,000 Expeditions and Econolines, it opted to shut the lines down.
Expedition production was restarted Feb. 12 with rear seats from Lear. Ford supplied front seats by increasing production at its Chesterfield, Mich., trim plant.
Johnson Controls' stock gained 87.5 cents to $86.25 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Ford was unchanged at $32.75, also on the NYSE.
